title: Fit a filled oxygen bubble humidifier onto a flowmeter outlet: square on the thread, hand-tight, never cross-threaded
instruction: Put the humidifier bottle on the oxygen flowmeter.
context: Category Other (oxygen therapy). "More than 1.5 million adults in the United States use supplemental oxygen" (ATS workshop report, Ann Am Thorac Soc 2018), and 14% of 55,208 patients in a UK national hospital audit were on oxygen (BTS 2017). At higher flows the oxygen is bubbled through a bottle of water screwed by its wing nut onto the oxygen source, the wall flowmeter in hospitals or the concentrator or liquid-oxygen unit at home (a DISS 1240, 9/16-18 thread). The maker warns: "Leaks may partially or fully reduce oxygen being delivered to the patient." (AirLife UG-20019), and Apria that cross-threading the cap lets oxygen escape out of the top of the bottle. One hand holds a 380 g bottle of water square under the outlet while the other turns the quad wing nut about two and a half turns, a quarter turn per stroke; then the bottle must be let go to hang from the thread.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Flowmeter: a 0-15 L/min wall oxygen flowmeter (body 9 x 6 x 18 cm) on a plywood mock wall 18 mm thick, 14 cm wide and 45 cm tall whose front face is at x 44.0; its outlet is a DISS 1240 oxygen connection, a 9/16-18 UNF male thread (14.29 mm, 1.411 mm pitch) 8 mm long under a 22 mm hex body 16 mm tall, pointing straight down on the axis x 36.0, y 0.0, the hex body's underside at z 21.85. Humidifier: an AirLife (Salter Labs) 7600 bubble humidifier, 350 cc, 6 psi pop-off: 3.25 in (82.6 mm) across the lid, 7.00 in (178 mm) tall to the mouth of its quad wing nut (46 mm across the wings), a 66 mm jar; filled to its maximum line, 290 mL (380 g with the 90 g bottle). It stands upright on the table at (38.0, -14.0), lid closed, a wing of its nut pointing at the robot's left (+y). Both arms start at their ready pose. What is simulated, and how, is in README.md.
scoring: The trial's score is the one at its last step. It scores 1.0 when the wing nut is seated on the outlet, the bottle hangs from the outlet with no part of either arm touching the bottle or its nut (in simulation every arm link at least 5 mm clear), and all is still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s. It scores 0.5 when the nut is seated but the bottle is not yet let go or still, and 0.25 when at the end the nut is square on the thread (its axis within 0.6 mm and 2 degrees of the outlet's), at least a full turn on (within 1.29 mm of its seat), but not seated. Otherwise it scores 0, and always 0 once any of these happened: the nut cross-threaded (in simulation: turned at least a quarter turn onto the thread, its axis within 3 mm of the outlet's and tilted more than 3.0 degrees off it, the thread's cross-threading angle atan(P/2 / pitch diameter)); the bottle dropped (falling faster than 0.4 m/s); the bottle tipped past 83 degrees, where its 290 mL reaches the gas passage under the lid. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Seated: in simulation read from the nut's own pose on the outlet: its turn within 45 degrees of the seated turn, within half the 1.411 mm pitch of its seat, its axis within 0.6 mm and 2 degrees of the outlet's. Real trial, checked in this order after the trial, the nut never loosened: (1) square: against a square stood on the table, front and side, the jar's gap to the blade differs by under 4 mm over its 125 mm (2 degrees); a cross-threaded nut hangs it more than 3 degrees off (over 6.5 mm). (2) Turns: a tester, steadying the bottle, pencils a line across a wing and the hex body, then turns the wing nut on with the fingertips to its stop, counting turns by the line. Seated: it stops within an eighth of a turn, no thread showing between the nut and the hex body. 0.25 (loose but started square): it turns on freely more than an eighth and under 0.91 of a turn (1.29 mm) and then seats, square, no thread showing. A cross-threaded nut binds short of its seat with thread showing. A nut that turns on 0.91 of a turn or more scores 0. (3) Leak, only after (2) has turned the nut home: a blood-pressure bulb and gauge on a tube to the fitting's inlet, the humidifier's outlet port blocked with a fingertip, pumped to 200 mmHg (under the 6 psi pop-off), holds for 10 s; a nut started square seals once home, a cross-threaded one leaks. Any score above 0 needs (1) under 4 mm. Cross-threaded (0): over 6.5 mm in (1), binding in (2), leaking in (3), or seen in the video forced on at least a quarter turn while visibly tilted, even if straightened later. Dropped, tipped and let go: from the video. A trial stopped by the operator scores 0.
reset_notes: Each trial: fill the 7600 (a new one after any cross-threaded trial) to its maximum line (290 mL) with tap water, screw its lid on with the threads aligned, weigh it (380 g), stand it at its mark with a wing of the nut pointing at the robot's left. After the trial do the square, turns and leak checks, unscrew the bottle and stand it back at its mark: about a minute. In simulation the bottle always starts at its mark, filled.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The outlet's and the nut's threads are helices of convex hulls with the Unified 60-degree section at the 9/16-18 size, so the nut goes on only by turning and holds the bottle by thread contact alone; a tilted nut cannot reach its seat. The rigid threads cannot be damaged, so cross-threading is judged by tilt (over 3.0 degrees a quarter turn on). The nut swivels on the lid's tower (a revolute joint, as on the real bottle). The water is a rigid 290 g mass, not a fluid.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (3,600 steps, the run limit); demo: 1.0 (1,835 steps)
